senses.gloss: Messy and not taken care of, said of hair, clothes or a yard.
examples: He showed up for the interview in an *unkempt* suit.
Her hair was *unkempt* and her eyes were red.
The yard grew *more unkempt* every week the family was away.

senses.gloss: Saying or doing things that hurt people.
examples: It was *unkind* of you to laugh at her accent.
Don't be *unkind* to your little brother.
That was the *unkindest* thing anyone has ever said to me.

contrast: *Unknowing* describes the person who doesn't realize; the adverb *unknowingly* describes the act: *he unknowingly signed away his rights*.

senses.gloss: Not aware of what is really going on.
examples: The scam used *unknowing* students to move the money.
She was an *unknowing* witness to the whole argument.
Tourists make *unknowing* mistakes that the locals find funny.

contrast: American English writes one *l*: *unlabeled*. British books print *unlabelled*.

senses.gloss: Having no label or name on it.
examples: There were three *unlabeled* jars at the back of the fridge.
Never open an *unlabeled* file from a stranger.
Half the boxes in the garage are still *unlabeled*.

contrast: *Illegal* is the everyday word. *Unlawful* belongs to legal language and to fixed phrases: *unlawful entry*, *unlawful detention*.

senses.gloss: Against the law.
examples: The court found the search *unlawful*.
He was charged with *unlawful* possession of a firearm.
Firing someone for reporting a safety problem is *unlawful*.

contrast: The *lead* here is the metal, said like *led*, so the word rhymes with *shredded*. At the pump Americans also use it as a noun: *fill it up with unleaded*.

senses.gloss: Made without added lead, said of gasoline.
examples: Most cars built after 1975 need *unleaded* gas.
The station sells three grades of *unleaded* fuel.
Older engines were never designed to run on *unleaded* gasoline.

contrast: American English spells both the noun and the verb *license*, so the adjective is *unlicensed*; British English writes the noun *licence*.

senses.gloss: Without the official permit the law requires.
examples: An *unlicensed* contractor did the wiring, and it shows.
The city shut down two *unlicensed* day care centers.
Practicing medicine while *unlicensed* is a felony.

contrast: American English drops the *e*: *likable*, *unlikable*. *Unlikeable* is the British spelling.

senses.gloss: Hard to like.
examples: Every character in the novel is *unlikable* in a different way.
He isn't evil, just *unlikable*.
The remake made the hero *more unlikable* than the villain.

senses.gloss: With no limit on the amount, the number or the time.
examples: The plan comes with *unlimited* texting.
Kids get *unlimited* refills at that diner.
Your access to the archive is *unlimited* for a year.

ru: не внесённый в справочник; доступный только по ссылке
contrast: An *unlisted* phone number is one the phone company keeps out of the directory; the British term is *ex-directory*.

senses.gloss: Kept out of a public directory or list.
examples: Her number is *unlisted*, so you'll have to email her.
The house is *unlisted*, which is why it never came up in my search.

senses.gloss: Visible only to people who have the link, said of a video or a page.
senses.ru: доступный только по ссылке, скрытый из поиска
examples: I made the video *unlisted* so only the family can watch it.
*Unlisted* posts don't show up in search results.

senses.gloss: Having no lights; dark.
examples: Don't walk home down that *unlit* alley.
The parking lot is *unlit* after midnight.

senses.gloss: Not burning, said of a candle or a cigarette.
examples: An *unlit* cigarette hung from his mouth.
The birthday candles were still *unlit* when we started singing.

contrast: American English drops the *e*: *livable*, *unlivable*. British books print *unliveable*.

senses.gloss: Impossible, or almost impossible, to live in.
examples: The mold made the apartment *unlivable*.
Rents like these make the city *unlivable* for teachers.
Every August the top floor gets *more unlivable*.

senses.gloss: Not fastened with a lock.
examples: She left the back door *unlocked* again.
An *unlocked* bike downtown won't last an hour.

senses.gloss: Not tied to one carrier, said of a phone.
examples: I bought an *unlocked* phone so I could switch plans.
Is the phone *unlocked*, or is it still on a contract?

senses.gloss: Getting no love or affection from anyone.
examples: No child should grow up feeling *unloved*.
The old piano sat *unloved* in the corner of the basement.
He felt *more unloved* after the divorce than he ever had as a kid.

senses.gloss: Having bad luck.
examples: We were *unlucky* with the weather all week.
She was *unlucky* to hit every red light on Main Street.
He is the *unluckiest* driver I know.

senses.gloss: Believed to bring bad luck.
examples: Some hotels skip the thirteenth floor because the number is *unlucky*.
My grandmother thinks it's *unlucky* to open an umbrella indoors.

position: both — *an unmade bed* is far more common than *the bed is unmade*
contrast: It goes with beds and almost nothing else. For a room that hasn't been tidied, say *the room is a mess*, not *the room is unmade*.

senses.gloss: Not straightened out after being slept in, said of a bed.
examples: He left for work with an *unmade* bed, as usual.
The camera panned across a messy room and an *unmade* bed.
Housekeeping never leaves an *unmade* bed behind.

senses.gloss: Too big, too difficult or too wild to control.
examples: My hair gets *unmanageable* in humid weather.
The class became *unmanageable* the minute the substitute walked in.
The debt grew *more unmanageable* every month.

contrast: *Uncrewed* is now preferred at NASA and in science writing, but *an unmanned drone* is still what you hear on the news.

senses.gloss: Working with nobody on board or on duty.
examples: An *unmanned* aircraft photographed the fire.
The gate is *unmanned* after six, so bring your badge.
NASA sent several *unmanned* probes to Mars first.

senses.gloss: Carrying no sign, label or markings that would identify it.
examples: An *unmarked* police car pulled us over.
The trail is *unmarked* past the river, so bring a map.
They buried him in an *unmarked* grave.

contrast: Forms and conversation usually offer *single*. *Unmarried* is the more formal word and the one used in *an unmarried couple* living together.

senses.gloss: Not married.
examples: Both of my uncles are *unmarried*.
The form asks whether you are married or *unmarried*.
An *unmarried* couple bought the house next door.

contrast: For socks and shoes Americans usually say *mismatched*. On its own, *unmatched* almost always means *better than all the rest*.

senses.gloss: Better than anything else of its kind.
examples: Her record in the 400 meters is still *unmatched*.
The view from the top of the ridge is *unmatched*.

senses.gloss: Not forming a pair.
examples: He wore two *unmatched* socks to school.
There is a whole drawer of *unmatched* gloves by the door.

contrast: Watch the spelling: the final *e* of *mistake* drops out — *unmistakable*, not *unmistakeable*.

senses.gloss: So clear that you cannot be wrong about it.
senses.ru: безошибочный, ни с чем не спутаешь
examples: There was an *unmistakable* smell of gas in the hallway.
Her handwriting is *unmistakable*.
The look on his face was *unmistakable* — he had forgotten.

position: attributive only — *an unmitigated disaster*, never *the disaster was unmitigated*
contrast: It nearly always sits in front of a bad noun: *an unmitigated disaster*, *an unmitigated failure*, *unmitigated nonsense*.

senses.gloss: Complete, with nothing to soften it.
examples: Opening night was an *unmitigated* disaster.
Calling the merger an *unmitigated* failure is putting it kindly.
What he wrote in that letter was *unmitigated* nonsense.

senses.gloss: Having no desire to work or make an effort.
examples: By March the whole class was tired and *unmotivated*.
He isn't lazy, just *unmotivated* by this particular job.
Working from home left her *more unmotivated* than she expected.

position: predicative only — *she was unmoved*, not *an unmoved judge*

senses.gloss: Feeling no emotion or pity about something.
examples: The jury seemed *unmoved* by his apology.
She listened to the whole story *unmoved*.
Voters were *unmoved* by the last-minute ads.

position: both — usually before a noun: *an unnamed source*

senses.gloss: Whose name is not given.
examples: Two *unnamed* officials confirmed the story.
The money came from an *unnamed* donor.
The buyer wishes to stay *unnamed*.

senses.gloss: Not normal; going against the way things usually are.
examples: The room was filled with an *unnatural* silence.
Eighty degrees in February feels *unnatural*.

senses.gloss: Forced; not the way a person really behaves.
examples: His laugh sounded *unnatural* on camera.
She held the smile so long that it looked *unnatural*.
Reading from a script makes some people sound *more unnatural* than they really are.

contrast: Russian speakers often reach for *needless*. *Unnecessary* is the everyday word; *needless* survives mainly in *needless to say*.

senses.gloss: Not needed.
examples: The surgery turned out to be *unnecessary*.
You made an *unnecessary* trip — I could have emailed it.
All that shouting was completely *unnecessary*.

position: predicative only — almost always after *go*, *pass* or *slip*: *the typo went unnoticed*
contrast: It lives in the pattern *go unnoticed* or *pass unnoticed*. Before a noun it sounds wrong: say *a mistake nobody caught*, not *an unnoticed mistake*.

senses.gloss: Not seen or noticed by anyone.
examples: The typo went *unnoticed* until the book was printed.
She slipped out of the party *unnoticed*.
A leak that size does not stay *unnoticed* for long.

senses.gloss: With nothing standing in the way.
examples: The room has an *unobstructed* view of the lake.
Keep the fire exit *unobstructed* at all times.
From row A the stage is completely *unobstructed*.

senses.gloss: Not attracting attention; quiet and easy to ignore.
examples: The security cameras are small and *unobtrusive*.
A good waiter is friendly but *unobtrusive*.
We picked the *most unobtrusive* table in the room.

senses.gloss: Empty; with nobody living in it or using it.
examples: The house has been *unoccupied* since spring.
Take any *unoccupied* seat in the back.
Two offices on that floor are still *unoccupied*.

contrast: *Unofficial* means *not confirmed by whoever is in charge*; *informal* means *relaxed in style*. An *unofficial* count is not yet certified; an *informal* dinner has no dress code.

senses.gloss: Not confirmed or approved by the people in charge.
examples: The *unofficial* count has her ahead by two hundred votes.
Sunday practice is *unofficial*, so nobody has to come.
He is the team's *unofficial* captain.

senses.gloss: Still sealed or closed; never opened.
examples: There is an *unopened* bottle of wine in the pantry.
Her mail sat *unopened* for two weeks.
The store takes returns only on *unopened* boxes.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *she ran unopposed*

senses.gloss: With nobody competing against you or arguing against it.
examples: She ran *unopposed* for a second term.
The motion passed *unopposed*.
The bill cleared the committee *unopposed*.

contrast: For a messy person or room, *disorganized* is the usual word. *Unorganized* is common in American speech and is the standard term for workers with no union: *an unorganized workforce*.

senses.gloss: Not arranged or planned; without any order.
examples: My notes for this class are completely *unorganized*.
The move was *unorganized* from the first day.
Their closet is *more unorganized* than mine, which is saying something.

senses.gloss: Copied from, or too much like, something that already exists.
examples: The plot is *unoriginal*, but the acting is good.
My costume was *unoriginal* — three other people came as pirates.
Nothing is *more unoriginal* than a band name that starts with *The*.

contrast: Lowercase *unorthodox* just means *done in an unusual way*. Capitalized *Orthodox* names a church or a branch of Judaism — a different word.

senses.gloss: Not done the usual way.
examples: She has an *unorthodox* pitching motion that somehow works.
His teaching methods are *unorthodox* but effective.
The *most unorthodox* solution turned out to be the cheapest.

senses.gloss: Not yet paid, said of a bill or a debt.
examples: Two invoices from March are still *unpaid*.
They shut off the water over an *unpaid* bill.

senses.gloss: Done without pay, said of work or leave.
examples: She took three months of *unpaid* leave.
Most of the campaign staff were *unpaid* volunteers.

form: un- + *palatable*, from *palate* 'the roof of the mouth'

senses.gloss: Unpleasant to eat.
examples: The soup was cold and frankly *unpalatable*.
Hospital food has an *unpalatable* reputation.

senses.gloss: Hard to accept.
examples: The report contains some *unpalatable* facts about the school.
Both options were *unpalatable*, so we waited.
The longer he stalled, the *more unpalatable* the choices became.

contrast: Watch the spelling: one *r*, two *l*'s in the middle, one *l* at the end — *un-par-al-leled*.

senses.gloss: Greater or better than anything else of its kind.
examples: The museum has an *unparalleled* collection of Native American baskets.
She brings *unparalleled* energy to the job.
The storm caused damage *unparalleled* in the county's history.

contrast: American spelling ends in *-ized*; British books print *unpasteurised*.

senses.gloss: Not heated to kill bacteria, said of milk, juice or cheese.
examples: *Unpasteurized* milk cannot be sold across state lines.
The cheese is made from *unpasteurized* goat's milk.
Doctors tell pregnant women to avoid anything *unpasteurized*.

contrast: In American English the first syllable rhymes with *pay*: *uhn-pay-tree-AH-tik*. British speakers say *pat-* instead.

senses.gloss: Showing no loyalty to your country, or seeming not to.
examples: Criticizing a war is not *unpatriotic*.
He was called *unpatriotic* for refusing to stand.
Nothing is *more unpatriotic*, she argued, than lying to voters.

senses.gloss: Not covered with asphalt or concrete.
examples: The last two miles of the road are *unpaved*.
An *unpaved* driveway leads up to the cabin.
Half the streets in the old town are still *unpaved*.

senses.gloss: Calm; not worried or upset by what is happening.
examples: The cat sat *unperturbed* while the dog barked at it.
She was *unperturbed* by the boos from the crowd.
He looked *unperturbed* when the lights went out.

senses.gloss: Not arranged in advance; happening by chance.
examples: We made an *unplanned* stop in Memphis.
The pregnancy was *unplanned* but very welcome.
The best parts of the trip were all *unplanned*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to play on, said of a field or a golf lie.
examples: Three days of rain left the field *unplayable*.
His ball came to rest in a bush, *unplayable*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to play, said of a game, a disc or a recording.
examples: The game shipped so buggy that it was *unplayable* for a month.
The old DVD is scratched and *unplayable*.

senses.gloss: Not enjoyable; leaving you with a bad feeling.
examples: There was an *unpleasant* smell coming from the basement.
That flight was the *most unpleasant* six hours of my life.

senses.gloss: Rude or unfriendly, said of a person.
examples: The clerk was openly *unpleasant* to everyone in line.
He can be *unpleasant* when he hasn't slept.

senses.gloss: Not made smooth or shiny.
examples: *Unpolished* floors show every scratch.
The stone is *unpolished*, so it looks dull until you wet it.

senses.gloss: Rough; not yet worked into finished shape.
examples: The draft is *unpolished*, but the argument is all there.
His delivery is *unpolished*, and audiences like him for it.
Her early songs were *more unpolished* and, some say, better.

senses.gloss: Disliked by most people.
examples: The new tax was *unpopular* with almost everyone.
She made the *unpopular* decision to cancel the trip.
The mayor is *more unpopular* now than when she took office.

contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable and the vowel is short: *uhn-PRES-i-den-tid*, never *un-pre-SEE-*.

senses.gloss: Never having happened before.
examples: The city saw *unprecedented* flooding in October.
She won three titles in one year, an *unprecedented* run.
Demand for the vaccine was *unprecedented*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to know in advance; changing without warning.
examples: Mountain weather in April is *unpredictable*.
He is a good player but *unpredictable* under pressure.
The market has been *more unpredictable* than usual this year.

senses.gloss: Not ready for what is about to happen.
examples: We were completely *unprepared* for the cold.
He walked into the exam *unprepared*.
She was *unprepared* to answer questions about the layoffs.

senses.gloss: Simple and modest; not trying to seem important.
examples: It's an *unpretentious* little diner with very good pie.
For a famous writer he is remarkably *unpretentious*.
The *most unpretentious* house on the street is also the oldest.

senses.gloss: Willing to do wrong things to get what you want.
examples: An *unprincipled* landlord will find a way around the rule.
The whole campaign was *unprincipled* from the first week.
He is the *most unprincipled* person I have ever worked for.

senses.gloss: Not changed from its natural state, said of food.
examples: The diet is built around *unprocessed* foods.
*Unprocessed* oats take longer to cook than instant ones.

senses.gloss: Not yet dealt with, said of paperwork or data.
examples: Thousands of claims are still *unprocessed*.
My refund sat *unprocessed* for six weeks.

senses.gloss: Producing little or nothing useful.
examples: The meeting was two *unproductive* hours.
Arguing about who is to blame is *unproductive*.
That was the *most unproductive* week I have had all year.

contrast: In American English it is almost always about behavior, not skill. Someone who does poor work is *incompetent*; someone who shouts at a client is *unprofessional*.

senses.gloss: Not meeting the standards of behavior expected at work.
examples: Yelling at a customer is *unprofessional*.
The email was *unprofessional* and a little cruel.
Nothing looks *more unprofessional* than a typo in the subject line.

senses.gloss: Not making money.
examples: They closed three *unprofitable* stores.
The airline's shortest routes are the *most unprofitable*.
Farming that land is *unprofitable* without subsidies.

contrast: The adverb *unpromptedly* exists but is rare; Americans use the adjective where Russian would use an adverb: *he offered to help, unprompted*.

senses.gloss: Done without anyone asking or suggesting it.
examples: He offered to pay, completely *unprompted*.
An *unprompted* apology means more than one you had to ask for.
She named all fifty states *unprompted*.

contrast: Keep the *e* of *pronounce* before *-able*: *pronounceable*, *unpronounceable*.

senses.gloss: Too difficult to say out loud.
examples: The ingredient list is full of *unpronounceable* chemicals.
Her last name is beautiful and, for most Americans, *unpronounceable*.
He gave the dog an *unpronounceable* Welsh name.

senses.gloss: With nothing to keep it safe from harm.
examples: Don't leave your laptop *unprotected* on an open network.
The beach is *unprotected* from the north wind.
*Unprotected* seedlings won't survive a frost.

contrast: *Unproven* and *unproved* are both correct, but *unproven* is far more common in American writing.

senses.gloss: Not shown to be true.
examples: The claim is *unproven* and probably false.
*Unproven* remedies sell very well online.

senses.gloss: Not yet tested in real conditions.
examples: The team is starting an *unproven* quarterback.
They bet the company on an *unproven* technology.

senses.gloss: Happening without anything being done to cause it.
examples: It was an *unprovoked* attack on a man waiting for a bus.
The report lists six *unprovoked* shark encounters last year.
Her outburst was sudden and *unprovoked*.

senses.gloss: Not printed or made public.
examples: Three of her novels are still *unpublished*.
The library bought a box of *unpublished* letters.
The study remains *unpublished* two years after it was finished.

position: predicative only — almost always after *go*: *the crime went unpunished*
contrast: It lives in the pattern *go unpunished*. Before a noun it sounds wrong: say *a crime nobody was punished for*.

senses.gloss: Not punished.
examples: The vandalism went *unpunished*.
No good deed goes *unpunished*.
He can't let an insult go *unpunished*.

contrast: Two almost opposite feelings. After a verb it means *not trained enough*: *he is unqualified*. Before a noun like *success* or *support* it means *total*: *an unqualified success*.

senses.gloss: Not having the training, skills or right to do something.
examples: He is *unqualified* for the job and everyone knows it.
An *unqualified* aide was left in charge of the class.
She is *unqualified* to give medical advice.

senses.gloss: Complete, with nothing held back.
examples: The concert was an *unqualified* success.
She gave the plan her *unqualified* support.

senses.gloss: Certain; impossible to doubt.
examples: Her talent is *unquestionable*.
The evidence for the link is by now *unquestionable*.
He has an *unquestionable* right to see the file.

contrast: Don't mix it up with *unquestionable*. *Unquestioning loyalty* is loyalty that never asks why; *unquestionable loyalty* is loyalty nobody can doubt.

senses.gloss: Accepting something completely, without ever asking why.
examples: The group demands *unquestioning* loyalty.
He gave the coach four years of *unquestioning* obedience.
*Unquestioning* trust in a website is how people get scammed.

ru: не входящий в рейтинг, без места в рейтинге

senses.gloss: Not among the teams or players on the official ranking list.
examples: An *unranked* team beat the number two seed.
She was *unranked* coming into the tournament.
The Tigers open the season *unranked* for the first time in years.

senses.gloss: Impossible to get to or touch.
examples: The nest sits on an *unreachable* ledge.
The top shelf is *unreachable* without a stool.

senses.gloss: Impossible to contact.
examples: She's *unreachable* until Monday morning.
The server was *unreachable* all afternoon.

contrast: Here *read* is the past participle, said like *red*: *uhn-RED*, never *uhn-REED*. The related *unreadable* does use the long vowel.

senses.gloss: Not read by anyone.
examples: I have four hundred *unread* emails.
The report sat *unread* on his desk for a month.
Mark all the messages as *unread*.

contrast: Note the vowel change: *unread* is *uhn-RED*, but *unreadable* is *uhn-REE-duh-buhl*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to make out.
examples: His handwriting is *unreadable*.
The disk is damaged and *unreadable*.

senses.gloss: Too dull or too difficult to get through.
examples: The manual is technically accurate and completely *unreadable*.
It is the *most unreadable* book on the syllabus.

contrast: In casual American speech *unreal* is praise: *that concert was unreal* means it was fantastic.

senses.gloss: Not real, or too strange to feel real.
examples: Everything about that week felt *unreal*.
The colors in the photo look *unreal*.

senses.gloss: Amazing — informal.
examples: The view from the summit was *unreal*.
That catch in the ninth inning was *unreal*.

senses.gloss: Not sensible about what is actually possible.
examples: The deadline is *unrealistic*.
It's *unrealistic* to expect a reply the same day.
Their budget was *more unrealistic* than the schedule.

contrast: American spelling ends in *-ized*; British books print *unrealised*.

senses.gloss: Never achieved or developed.
examples: The whole article is about *unrealized* potential.
His plan for the park is one more *unrealized* dream.

senses.gloss: Existing on paper but not yet turned into cash, said of gains or losses.
examples: You owe no tax on *unrealized* gains.
The fund is carrying a large *unrealized* loss.

senses.gloss: Not fair or sensible.
examples: Her boss makes *unreasonable* demands.
It isn't *unreasonable* to ask for two days' notice.
He gets *more unreasonable* the later the meeting runs.

senses.gloss: Far greater than is fair, said of a price or an amount.
examples: They charge an *unreasonable* amount for parking.
The rent increase was plainly *unreasonable*.

contrast: American spelling uses *z*: *unrecognizable*. British books print *unrecognisable*.

senses.gloss: So changed that you cannot tell what or who it is.
examples: Downtown is *unrecognizable* after ten years away.
He shaved his beard and was almost *unrecognizable*.
The fire left the car *unrecognizable*.

senses.gloss: Not noticed or identified.
examples: The disease often goes *unrecognized* for years.
She walked through the hotel lobby *unrecognized*.

senses.gloss: Not officially accepted.
examples: The territory is an *unrecognized* state.
His degree is *unrecognized* in the United States.

senses.gloss: Impossible to get back.
examples: The files on the burned drive are *unrecoverable*.
Once you empty the trash, deleted photos may be *unrecoverable*.
Most of that loan is *unrecoverable*.

senses.gloss: Not processed; still close to its natural state.
examples: The recipe calls for *unrefined* coconut oil.
*Unrefined* sugar keeps more of the molasses.

senses.gloss: Rough; lacking polish or good manners.
examples: His humor is *unrefined* but never mean.
She thought their taste in furniture was *unrefined*.
The earlier draft was *more unrefined*, and funnier for it.

senses.gloss: Not entered on an official list.
examples: Driving an *unregistered* car will get you a ticket.
Thousands of eligible voters are still *unregistered*.
The gun turned out to be *unregistered*.

senses.gloss: Not controlled by government rules.
examples: The supplement industry is largely *unregulated*.
*Unregulated* lending helped cause the crash.
He worries about an *unregulated* market for these chemicals.

senses.gloss: Done without practicing it first.
examples: The interview was completely *unrehearsed*.
They gave an *unrehearsed* performance and it worked.
Her answer sounded *unrehearsed*, which is why people believed it.

ru: не связанный; не состоящий в родстве

senses.gloss: Not connected with something else.
examples: The two cases are *unrelated*.
She quit for reasons *unrelated* to the lawsuit.
On an *unrelated* note, did anyone fix the printer?

senses.gloss: Not from the same family.
senses.ru: не родственный, не состоящий в родстве
examples: The two Smiths in my class are *unrelated*.
They share a last name but are *unrelated*.

senses.gloss: Not yet made available to the public.
examples: The album includes two *unreleased* tracks.
Fans trade *unreleased* demos online.
The movie has been finished but *unreleased* for two years.

senses.gloss: Never stopping or getting any weaker.
examples: The heat in August was *unrelenting*.
She faced *unrelenting* pressure from the board.
His critics have been *unrelenting*.

senses.gloss: Not to be trusted to work, to be true, or to do what was promised.
examples: The bus out to the airport is *unreliable*.
He is a warm person but an *unreliable* friend.
That website is the *most unreliable* source on the list.

senses.gloss: Ordinary; with nothing about it worth noticing.
examples: From the street it's an *unremarkable* brick building.
The meal was pleasant and *unremarkable*.
He has one of the *most unremarkable* faces I have ever seen.

contrast: *Unremitting* and *unrelenting* mean much the same thing, but *unremitting* is the more formal, more bookish of the two.

senses.gloss: Continuing without a break, usually of something hard to bear.
examples: Three weeks of *unremitting* rain flooded the fields.
The job demands *unremitting* attention to detail.
They lived under *unremitting* pressure to sell the farm.

senses.gloss: Not sorry for something you did wrong.
examples: He was *unrepentant* at his sentencing.
She is *unrepentant* about the post.
The paper called him an *unrepentant* liar.

senses.gloss: Not told to the authorities or to the public.
examples: Most cases of the illness go *unreported*.
He had thousands of dollars in *unreported* income.
The crash stayed *unreported* for a week.

position: both — almost always before a noun, in the phrase *unrequited love*
form: un- + *requited*, from the old verb *requite* 'to return in kind'
contrast: You will meet it in one phrase, *unrequited love*, and hardly anywhere else.

senses.gloss: Not returned, said of love or affection.
examples: The whole album is about *unrequited* love.
He spent a year on an *unrequited* crush.
Her affection for him was *unrequited*.

senses.gloss: Not settled or decided.
examples: The dispute is still *unresolved*.
There are two *unresolved* questions in the report.
He left the meeting with a lot of *unresolved* anger.

senses.gloss: Not answering or reacting to people.
examples: The agency has been *unresponsive* to every complaint.
He sat *unresponsive* through the whole meeting.

senses.gloss: Not reacting to treatment, to input, or to anything at all.
senses.ru: не поддающийся (лечению); не реагирующий; без сознания
examples: The tumor was *unresponsive* to chemotherapy.
The touchscreen goes *unresponsive* in cold weather.
Paramedics found her *unresponsive* on the kitchen floor.

senses.gloss: Not held back or kept under control.
examples: The crowd greeted her with *unrestrained* cheering.
He wrote about the trip with *unrestrained* joy.
Her anger that night was completely *unrestrained*.

senses.gloss: With no rules limiting it.
examples: Members get *unrestricted* access to the archive.
The grant money is *unrestricted*, so we can spend it where it's needed.
*Unrestricted* travel between the two countries resumed in June.

senses.gloss: Not yet ready to eat or pick.
examples: The peaches at the store were hard and *unripe*.
*Unripe* tomatoes are good fried.
The fruit at the bottom of the box was *more unripe* than the rest.

contrast: American English writes one *l*: *unrivaled*. British books print *unrivalled*.

senses.gloss: Better than anything or anyone else of its kind.
examples: The store has an *unrivaled* selection of used records.
Her knowledge of the river is *unrivaled*.
For pure speed the train is *unrivaled*.

contrast: It ends in *-ly* but it is an adjective, not an adverb — like *friendly* and *lonely*. There is no adverb *unrulily*; say *in an unruly way*.

senses.gloss: Hard to control, said of a person or a crowd.
examples: An *unruly* fan was escorted out in the third inning.
The class got *unruly* right after lunch.
It was the *unruliest* crowd the arena had seen all year.

senses.gloss: Sticking out and hard to comb, said of hair.
examples: He pushed his *unruly* hair out of his eyes.
*Unruly* curls run in the family.
